n.1: Maltase splits maltose into two glucose molecules; it does not act on sucrose.
n.2: Lactase splits lactose (milk sugar) into glucose and galactose; sucrose is digested by sucrase.

AP.q: A classmate claims that epithelial tissue and every kind of connective tissue are supplied directly by blood vessels. Which correction is accurate?
o: Bone and blood are avascular and are nourished by diffusion
Cartilage is vascular, but epithelium is nourished by diffusion
Epithelium and cartilage are both avascular and fed by diffusion
Epithelium is vascular, but cartilage is nourished by diffusion
AP.w: Epithelial tissue is avascular and is fed by diffusion from underlying connective tissue. Most connective tissue is vascular, but cartilage is an avascular exception.

n.0: Bone is a vascular connective tissue, and blood flows inside vessels as the fluid connective tissue.
n.1: Cartilage is the avascular connective tissue; this option reverses the facts for both tissues.
n.3: Epithelium has no blood vessels between its cells; it relies on diffusion from the tissue below.

AP.q: A nurse asks a patient to raise the arm out to the side until it is level with the shoulder. Which muscle is the prime mover for this abduction of the arm?
AP.w: The deltoid, which caps the shoulder, is the prime mover of arm abduction (moving the arm away from the midline). It is also a common intramuscular injection site.

n.0: The pectoralis major flexes, adducts and medially rotates the arm.
n.1: The latissimus dorsi extends and adducts the arm, the opposite direction to abduction.
n.2: The trapezius elevates and retracts the scapula and extends the head; it does not abduct the arm at the shoulder joint.

AP.q: Which layer of the heart wall is also called the visceral layer of the serous pericardium?
AP.w: The epicardium is the visceral layer of the serous pericardium: it lies directly on the heart's surface, with pericardial fluid between it and the parietal layer.

n.0: The endocardium lines the chambers and valves on the inside of the heart.
n.1: The fibrous pericardium is the tough outermost sac, not a serous layer on the heart.
n.2: The parietal pericardium lines the inside of the fibrous sac; visceral means on the organ itself.

AP.q: After drinking several beers at a party, a woman produces a large volume of pale, dilute urine. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: Alcohol inhibits ADH, so collecting ducts reclaim less water
Alcohol blocks glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule
Alcohol stimulates ADH, which increases urine output
Alcohol raises aldosterone, so more sodium is excreted
AP.w: Alcohol inhibits ADH release. With less ADH, fewer aquaporins sit in the collecting ducts, less water is reabsorbed, and a large volume of dilute urine results.

n.1: Blocked glucose reabsorption would put glucose in the urine; that is not how alcohol increases urine volume.
n.2: ADH reduces urine output; alcohol inhibits it rather than stimulating it.
n.3: Aldosterone causes sodium reabsorption, not sodium excretion.

AP.q: The radius and ulna are the two bones of the forearm. In anatomical position, which term describes the location of the radius relative to the ulna?
AP.w: In anatomical position the palms face forward, so the radius (on the thumb side) lies farther from the midline than the ulna. The radius is lateral to the ulna.

n.0: With the palms facing forward, the two bones lie side by side, not one behind the other.
n.2: Proximal and distal compare distance from the limb's attachment. The radius and ulna lie side by side along the same length of forearm.
n.3: The ulna (little-finger side) is the medial bone; the radius is lateral to it.

AP.q: Both B and T lymphocytes arise from stem cells in red bone marrow. Where does each type of lymphocyte complete its maturation before it can respond to antigens?
o: T cells in the thymus; B cells in red bone marrow
T cells in the lymph nodes; B cells in red bone marrow
T cells in the thymus; B cells in the spleen
T cells in red bone marrow; B cells in the thymus
AP.w: T cells mature in the thymus (T for thymus), and B cells mature in red bone marrow. These are the two primary lymphoid organs.

n.1: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs that house mature lymphocytes; T cells mature in the thymus.
n.2: The spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ where mature lymphocytes respond to antigens; B cells mature in red bone marrow.
n.3: This reverses the two sites: T cells mature in the thymus and B cells in red bone marrow.

AP.q: A researcher stimulates a neuron with a stimulus well above threshold and then with a stimulus twice as strong. How does the neuron's response to the stronger stimulus differ?
o: Action potentials fire more often; each is the same size
Each action potential is about twice as large
Action potentials keep the same rate, but each one lasts longer
Each action potential travels about twice as fast
AP.w: Action potentials are all-or-none: once threshold is reached, each one is the same size. A stronger stimulus increases how often action potentials fire, not their size.

n.1: Action potentials are all-or-none, so a stronger stimulus does not make each one larger.
n.2: Stimulus strength is coded by firing frequency; the rate rises rather than staying the same.
n.3: Conduction speed depends on the axon itself, such as whether it is myelinated, not on stimulus strength.

AP.q: Which plasma protein is the most abundant and is chiefly responsible for maintaining the osmotic pressure of the blood?
AP.w: Albumin, made by the liver, is the most abundant plasma protein; it holds water in the blood vessels by osmotic pressure.

n.0: Fibrinogen is the clotting protein that becomes fibrin.
n.1: Hemoglobin is inside red blood cells, not a plasma protein.
n.3: Globulins include antibodies and transport proteins; they are less abundant than albumin.

AP.q: Which structure in the wall of the heart normally acts as its natural pacemaker, setting a resting rate of about 60 to 100 impulses per minute?
AP.w: The sinoatrial (SA) node, in the wall of the right atrium, fires fastest (about 60 to 100 impulses per minute), so it sets the pace for the whole heart.

n.0: Purkinje fibers spread the impulse through the ventricles; their own intrinsic rate is much slower than the SA node's.
n.2: The bundle of His conducts the impulse from the AV node into the septum; it does not set the rate.
n.3: The AV node can take over as a backup pacemaker, but it fires more slowly than the SA node, so it does not normally set the rate.

AP.q: A patient eats a lunch of grilled chicken, which is mostly protein. In which organ does chemical digestion of this protein begin, and which enzyme starts it?
AP.w: Protein digestion begins in the stomach, where pepsin (activated from pepsinogen by hydrochloric acid) breaks proteins into shorter peptides. Carbohydrate digestion is the one that begins in the mouth.

n.0: Salivary amylase digests starch, not protein; protein digestion does not begin in the mouth.
n.1: Trypsin continues protein digestion in the small intestine after pepsin has started it in the stomach.
n.2: Lingual lipase acts on fats, and protein digestion does not begin in the mouth.

AP.q: Blood plasma belongs to which body fluid compartment, and which other fluid shares that compartment?
o: Extracellular fluid; cytosol of red cells
Intracellular fluid; cytosol of all cells
AP.w: Body water is split into intracellular fluid (inside cells, the larger share) and extracellular fluid. Extracellular fluid is plasma plus interstitial fluid, the fluid that bathes the cells in the tissues.

n.1: Interstitial fluid lies outside cells, and so does plasma, so neither belongs to the intracellular compartment.
n.2: Plasma is extracellular, but the cytosol inside red blood cells is intracellular fluid.
n.3: Cytosol is intracellular fluid, but plasma lies outside cells and is extracellular.

AP.q: A biopsy from the sole of the foot shows a clear layer of flattened dead cells between the stratum granulosum and the stratum corneum. A biopsy from the upper arm lacks it. Which layer is this?
AP.w: The stratum lucidum is a thin, clear layer between the granulosum and corneum that is present in the thick skin of the palms and soles and absent from thin skin.

n.0: The papillary layer is the superficial part of the dermis, below the whole epidermis.
n.1: The stratum spinosum lies below the granulosum and is present in both thick and thin skin.
n.2: The stratum basale is the deepest epidermal layer and is present in all skin.

AP.q: The intercostal muscles help lift the rib cage during breathing. Based on the word parts, where are these muscles located?
AP.w: inter- means between and cost/o means rib, so the intercostal muscles lie in the spaces between adjacent ribs.

n.0: Beneath would use sub- (subcostal); inter- means between.
n.1: The vertebrae use the root vertebr/o; cost/o means rib.
n.3: Within would use intra-; these muscles span the spaces between ribs, not the inside of the bones.

AP.q: After six months on a space station, an astronaut has lost bone density in the legs despite eating a normal diet. Which principle best explains this loss?
o: Bone remodels in response to the mechanical stress on it
Osteoclasts resorb bone when blood calcium rises above normal
Bone mass is fixed once the epiphyseal plates close
Calcitonin rises when the skeleton bears less weight
AP.w: Bone remodeling responds to mechanical stress (Wolff's law): weight-bearing load stimulates bone formation. Without load, resorption by osteoclasts exceeds formation by osteoblasts, so bone density falls.

n.1: High blood calcium triggers calcitonin, which inhibits osteoclasts; resorption is driven by low blood calcium (PTH) and, in this case, by the loss of mechanical load.
n.2: Bone is remodeled throughout life; adults gain or lose bone mass long after the growth plates close.
n.3: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts, so it would tend to preserve bone; it does not explain the loss.

AP.q: A patient's skin and the whites of the eyes both look yellow. Buildup of which pigment best explains this color change?
AP.w: Jaundice is a yellow color of the skin and the sclerae caused by bilirubin, a pigment formed when hemoglobin is broken down. Carotene can tint skin yellow-orange but does not yellow the sclerae.

n.0: Melanin is the brown-black pigment from melanocytes; more of it darkens the skin rather than turning it yellow.
n.1: Oxygenated hemoglobin gives skin a pink tone; too little oxygen causes a bluish color (cyanosis), not yellowing.
n.3: Carotene from orange and yellow vegetables can tint the skin yellow-orange, but it does not turn the whites of the eyes yellow.

AP.q: A semen analysis shows sperm with normal heads and tails but abnormal midpieces. Which function would be most directly impaired in these sperm?
o: Releasing enzymes that digest the oocyte's outer layers
Supplying the ATP that powers movement of the tail
Storing the fructose that sperm use as an energy source
Delivering 23 chromosomes to the oocyte at fertilization
AP.w: The midpiece is packed with mitochondria that make ATP to power the flagellum. A defective midpiece leaves the tail short of energy, reducing motility.

n.0: The penetrating enzymes sit in the acrosome on the head, which is normal here.
n.2: Fructose is supplied in seminal vesicle fluid; it is not stored in the sperm's midpiece.
n.3: The chromosomes are in the nucleus of the head, which is normal here.

AP.q: A medication works by binding to a receptor protein on the surface of liver cells. At which level of organization does the receptor protein itself belong?
o: Chemical, because a protein is a large molecule built from atoms
Cellular, because it sits on the plasma membrane of a cell
Tissue, because liver cells form a group with a shared function
Organ, because its effects change how the whole liver functions
AP.w: A protein is a molecule, and atoms and molecules make up the chemical level. Its location on a cell does not change its own level.

n.1: The receptor is part of a cell, but a part of a cell is not a cell. The protein is a molecule at the chemical level.
n.2: The liver cells together form a tissue, but the receptor protein on one cell is a molecule.
n.3: The drug's effect reaches the organ, but the receptor protein itself is a molecule at the chemical level.

AP.q: A physical therapist moves a patient's thigh through flexion, abduction, rotation and circumduction at the hip, then bends and straightens the elbow at the humeroulnar joint. Which pairing correctly classifies these two synovial joints?
AP.w: The hip is a ball-and-socket joint: the rounded femoral head sits in the cup-shaped acetabulum, allowing multiaxial movement including rotation and circumduction. The humeroulnar joint is a uniaxial hinge that allows flexion and extension; forearm rotation happens at the radioulnar joints, the proximal one being a pivot.

n.0: The humeroulnar joint is a hinge that allows only flexion and extension; the pivot joint at the elbow is the proximal radioulnar joint, which rotates the radius.
n.2: The hip is not condyloid: condyloid (ellipsoid) joints such as the wrist are biaxial and do not allow true rotation, which the hip performs.
n.3: Both are misclassified: a condyloid joint cannot rotate as the hip does, and the humeroulnar joint is a hinge, not the radioulnar pivot.

AP.q: After a fall from a ladder, a construction worker had a CT scan that ruled out intracranial bleeding. Based on its word parts, where would intracranial bleeding occur?
AP.w: intra- means within and crani/o means skull, so intracranial means inside the skull.

n.0: Between is inter-, the look-alike prefix.
n.1: Around is peri- or circum-.
n.2: Below is sub- or hypo-.

AP.q: Blood calcium drops below its normal range, and the parathyroid glands respond by increasing hormone secretion. What effect does this hormone have on bone tissue?
o: Osteoblast activity rises, depositing Ca²⁺ into the matrix
Osteoclast activity rises, releasing Ca²⁺ from the matrix
Osteoclast activity falls, keeping Ca²⁺ stored in the matrix
Calcitonin release rises, moving Ca²⁺ out of the matrix
AP.w: Step 1: low blood Ca²⁺ triggers release of parathyroid hormone (PTH). Step 2: PTH raises blood Ca²⁺ by stimulating osteoclast activity, which resorbs matrix and releases Ca²⁺ (bone stores about 99% of the body's calcium).

n.0: Osteoblast deposition would move calcium out of the blood and into bone, the opposite of what PTH achieves.
n.2: Reducing osteoclast activity lowers blood Ca²⁺, which matches calcitonin, not PTH.
n.3: Calcitonin comes from the thyroid gland, not the parathyroids, and it lowers blood calcium rather than releasing it from bone.

AP.q: A rise in blood volume triggers a hormone that makes the kidneys excrete more sodium and water, lowering blood pressure. Which hormone and source are correct?
AP.w: When high blood volume stretches the atria, atrial cells release ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide), which makes the kidneys excrete Na⁺ and water, lowering blood volume and pressure.

n.0: ADH makes the kidneys reabsorb water and reduces urine output; it is released when the body needs to keep water.
n.1: Renin is released by the juxtaglomerular cells when blood pressure is low and leads to aldosterone release, which raises blood pressure.
n.3: Aldosterone does the opposite: it makes the kidneys reabsorb Na⁺ (water follows), raising blood volume.

AP.q: A rare disorder damages the efferent fibers of the autonomic nervous system while sparing all other nerve fibers. Which function would be directly affected?
o: Changes in heart rate during exercise
Sensing stretch of a full stomach wall
Voluntary flexing of the elbow joint
Detection of pain from the skin of the hand
AP.w: Autonomic efferent (motor) fibers control cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands, so adjusting the heart rate would be lost. Sensory (afferent) fibers and somatic motor fibers are spared.

n.1: Sensing stretch is a sensory (afferent) function; the afferent fibers are spared.
n.2: Flexing the elbow uses skeletal muscle, which is controlled by somatic motor fibers that are spared.
n.3: Pain detection travels on afferent (sensory) fibers, which are spared.

AP.q: Which type of epithelium lines most of the trachea and bronchi and carries the cilia of the mucociliary escalator?
AP.w: The conducting airways are lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells: one layer of cells that looks layered, with cilia that sweep mucus upward.

n.0: Simple ciliated columnar epithelium is a true single layer of tall cells that lines the uterine tubes; the trachea and bronchi have the pseudostratified form, whose nuclei sit at different heights.
n.1: Cuboidal cells, some with cilia, line only the smallest bronchioles near the respiratory zone, not the trachea and bronchi.
n.3: Nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium resists abrasion in the oropharynx, laryngopharynx and esophagus; it has no cilia and does not line the trachea.

AP.q: Most homeostatic mechanisms use negative feedback, but a few use positive feedback. Which of the following is an example of positive feedback?
o: Oxytocin release that strengthens uterine contractions in labor
A slower heart rate that lowers a sudden rise in blood pressure
Insulin release that lowers blood glucose after a meal
Shivering that raises body temperature when it falls
AP.w: During childbirth, pressure on the cervix triggers oxytocin release, which strengthens contractions, which triggers more oxytocin. The change is amplified until the baby is delivered.

n.1: The baroreceptor reflex reverses a rise in blood pressure, which is negative feedback.
n.2: Insulin reverses a rise in blood glucose, which is negative feedback.
n.3: Shivering reverses a fall in body temperature, which is negative feedback.

AP.q: After a stroke, a patient cannot feel touch or temperature on his right hand, yet he can still move the hand normally. Which lobe is most likely damaged?
AP.w: The parietal lobe holds the somatosensory cortex, which perceives touch, pain, temperature and body position. Voluntary movement is controlled by the frontal lobe's primary motor cortex, which is spared here.

n.1: The occipital lobe processes vision, not touch or temperature.
n.2: The temporal lobe processes hearing and language comprehension, not touch.
n.3: The frontal lobe's primary motor cortex controls voluntary movement, which is intact in this patient.

AP.q: During a strong concentric contraction of the biceps brachii, which change occurs within each sarcomere of its fibers?
o: The H zone widens as the Z discs move apart
The A band shortens while the I band keeps its length
The I band and H zone shorten while the A band keeps its length
The actin and myosin filaments shorten as the Z discs move closer
AP.w: In the sliding filament model, thin actin filaments slide toward the M line: the Z discs move closer and the I band and H zone shorten. The A band equals the length of the thick myosin filaments, so it stays the same. The filaments slide; they do not shorten.

n.0: In contraction the H zone narrows and the Z discs move closer together, not apart.
n.1: The A band is the length of the myosin filaments, which do not shorten; it is the I band that narrows.
n.3: Neither filament shortens; actin and myosin slide past each other while keeping their lengths.

AP.q: A healthy adult's spirometry shows a tidal volume of 500 mL, an inspiratory reserve volume of 3,000 mL, an expiratory reserve volume of 1,100 mL and a residual volume of 1,200 mL. What is the vital capacity?
AP.w: Vital capacity = tidal volume + inspiratory reserve volume + expiratory reserve volume = 500 + 3,000 + 1,100 = 4,600 mL. Residual volume is not included because it cannot be exhaled.

n.0: 4,100 mL leaves out the tidal volume (3,000 + 1,100).
n.1: 5,800 mL adds the residual volume as well, which gives total lung capacity rather than vital capacity.
n.3: 3,500 mL is tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve volume only (the inspiratory capacity); the expiratory reserve volume is missing.

BI.q: On a quiz, a student writes that the Golgi apparatus makes proteins. Which correction describes the role of the Golgi accurately?
o: It breaks down proteins with hydrolytic enzymes.
It synthesizes lipids and steroid hormones.
It modifies and packages proteins made elsewhere.
It copies DNA into messenger RNA for export.
BI.w: Proteins are made by ribosomes (many on rough ER). The Golgi then modifies, sorts and packages them into vesicles, like a post office.

n.0: Breaking down material with hydrolytic enzymes is the job of lysosomes.
n.1: Lipid and steroid synthesis happens in the smooth ER.
n.3: Copying DNA into mRNA is transcription, which takes place in the nucleus.

BI.q: The inner membrane of a mitochondrion is folded into many cristae. What is the main advantage of this folding for the cell?
o: It anchors ribosomes that make secreted proteins.
It gives the electron transport chain more area.
It holds chlorophyll for capturing light energy.
It stores calcium ions for muscle contraction.
BI.w: The electron transport chain sits in the inner membrane (cristae) and makes most of the cell's ATP, so more folds mean more membrane for ATP production.

n.0: Ribosomes making secreted proteins are attached to the rough ER.
n.2: Chlorophyll is held in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts, not mitochondria.
n.3: Calcium storage for contraction is the job of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, a smooth ER in muscle.

BI.q: Liver cells of a patient who takes a daily anticonvulsant drug show a marked increase in an organelle that detoxifies drugs and makes lipids. Which organelle is it?
BI.w: Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and carries out lipid and steroid synthesis and detoxification, which is why it is prominent in liver cells exposed to drugs.

n.0: The Golgi modifies, sorts and packages proteins and lipids; it does not detoxify drugs.
n.2: Rough ER makes proteins on its ribosomes; detoxification and lipid synthesis are smooth ER jobs.
n.3: The nucleolus makes ribosomal RNA and assembles ribosome subunits inside the nucleus.

BI.q: Energy for a muscle contraction is released when a cell converts ATP into ADP and an inorganic phosphate. Which bond is broken in this reaction?
o: The bond between the first and second phosphates
The bond between ribose and the first phosphate
The bond holding the last phosphate group
The bond between adenine and ribose
BI.w: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) releases usable energy when the bond to its last (third) phosphate is hydrolyzed, giving ADP + Pi.

n.0: Breaking between the first and second phosphates would release two phosphates together and leave AMP, not ADP + Pi.
n.1: Losing the first phosphate would remove all three phosphates at once, not form ADP.
n.3: Breaking the adenine-ribose bond would destroy the nucleoside rather than form ADP.

BI.q: Heart muscle cells contract continuously throughout life and need a steady supply of ATP. Compared with less active cells, which organelle would these cells contain in especially large numbers?
BI.w: Mitochondria carry out aerobic cellular respiration and make most of a cell's ATP, so highly active cells such as cardiac and skeletal muscle cells contain many of them.

n.1: Lysosomes digest worn-out parts and engulfed particles; they do not supply ATP.
n.2: Peroxisomes break down fatty acids and hydrogen peroxide but are not the main ATP producers.
n.3: Ribosomes make proteins. ATP production is the job of mitochondria.

BI.q: A cell completely breaks down 3 molecules of glucose by aerobic respiration. How many molecules of carbon dioxide are released?
BI.w: C6H12O6 + 6 O2 -> 6 CO2 + 6 H2O, so each glucose releases 6 CO2: 3 x 6 = 18.

n.0: 12 CO2 corresponds to two glucose molecules, not three.
n.1: 6 CO2 is the amount for one glucose; the cell broke down three.
n.3: Each glucose has six carbons, so it releases six CO2, not one.

BI.q: In a family pedigree, two unaffected parents have a daughter who is affected by a rare genetic disorder. Which inheritance pattern and parental genotypes best fit this pedigree?
o: Autosomal dominant, with one parent a carrier
Autosomal recessive, with both parents carriers
X-linked recessive, with the father a carrier
X-linked recessive, with the mother a carrier
BI.w: Step 1: unaffected parents with an affected child means the trait is recessive and both parents carry it. Step 2: an affected daughter with an X-linked recessive trait would need an affected father, and this father is unaffected, so the pattern is autosomal recessive.

n.0: In autosomal dominant inheritance anyone with one copy is affected, so an affected child needs an affected parent.
n.2: A male has one X, so a father with the recessive allele would be affected, not a carrier, and an unaffected father gives his daughter a normal X.
n.3: For a daughter to have an X-linked recessive trait she needs the allele from her father too, which would make him affected.

BI.q: Under an electron microscope, a cell shows a plasma membrane, a cell wall, ribosomes and DNA in a nucleoid region, but no membrane-bound organelles. Which organism is the likely source?
o: A leaf cell from a pea plant
A yeast cell used to leaven bread
A bacterium such as Escherichia coli
BI.w: A nucleoid region in place of a nucleus and the absence of membrane-bound organelles mark a prokaryotic cell. Bacteria are prokaryotes, and most have a cell wall made of peptidoglycan.

n.0: A pea leaf cell has a cell wall, but as a eukaryote it has a nucleus, chloroplasts and mitochondria.
n.1: Yeast is a fungus, a eukaryote. It has a cell wall (chitin) but also a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles.
n.3: Giardia is a protozoan, a single-celled eukaryote with a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

BI.q: In a leaf cell, water molecules are split and oxygen gas is released during photosynthesis. Where in the chloroplast does this happen?
o: In the inner membrane, during electron transport
In the thylakoids, during the light reactions
In the stroma, during the Calvin cycle
BI.w: The light-dependent reactions take place in the thylakoid membranes. There water is split, O₂ is released, and ATP and NADPH are made for the Calvin cycle.

n.0: Electron transport on an inner membrane that ends with O₂ forming water describes mitochondria, the reverse of releasing O₂.
n.2: Glycolysis in the cytoplasm is part of respiration and neither splits water nor releases oxygen.
n.3: The Calvin cycle in the stroma fixes CO₂ into sugar; it does not split water.

BI.q: Which statement about energy conversions in cells agrees with the laws of thermodynamics?
o: Cell energy conversions lose no energy as heat.
Energy in ATP is destroyed when the ATP is used.
Cells create new energy when they break down glucose.
Each conversion releases some energy as heat.
BI.w: Energy is neither created nor destroyed, only converted, and every conversion loses some energy as heat (entropy increases).

n.0: No conversion is perfectly efficient; some energy always escapes as heat.
n.1: Energy cannot be destroyed; ATP's energy is transferred to cell work and heat.
n.2: Energy cannot be created; cells convert chemical energy already stored in glucose.

BI.q: During lactic acid fermentation in muscle, what does converting pyruvate to lactic acid accomplish for the cell?
o: It supplies oxygen to the electron transport chain.
It releases CO2 that feeds the Krebs cycle.
It makes most of the ATP the cell uses.
It regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can go on.
BI.w: Glycolysis needs NAD+. Without oxygen, turning pyruvate into lactic acid regenerates NAD+, so glycolysis keeps making its 2 ATP per glucose.

n.0: Fermentation makes no oxygen; it is how cells cope when oxygen is lacking.
n.1: Lactic acid fermentation releases no CO2, and the Krebs cycle stalls without oxygen.
n.2: Fermentation adds no ATP beyond the 2 from glycolysis; most ATP comes from the chain.

BI.q: A gardener crosses a red-flowered snapdragon with a white-flowered snapdragon, and every offspring plant has pink flowers. Which inheritance pattern does this show?
BI.w: In incomplete dominance the heterozygote shows a blended, intermediate phenotype: red x white gives pink.

n.0: In codominance both alleles show fully (red and white patches or hairs), not a blend.
n.1: Polygenic traits come from many genes and give a continuous range, not one uniform intermediate color.
n.3: Multiple alleles means a gene has more than two alleles in the population; this cross involves two alleles, and the term does not explain a blended heterozygote.

BI.q: A cancer drug blocks the assembly of microtubules from tubulin. Which cell process would this drug most directly interfere with?
o: Synthesis of steroids in the smooth ER
Production of ATP on the cristae
BI.w: Microtubules form the spindle fibers that move chromosomes during cell division, so blocking them stops dividing cells, which is why such drugs are used against cancer.

n.0: Steroid synthesis is carried out by smooth ER enzymes, not by the cytoskeleton.
n.2: ATP is made by the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane, not by microtubules.
n.3: Ribosomal RNA is made in the nucleolus and does not depend on microtubule assembly.

BI.q: A patient breathes in oxygen that eventually reaches the mitochondria of her cells. What is the role of this oxygen in aerobic cellular respiration?
o: It accepts electrons from the chain and forms water.
It splits glucose into two molecules of pyruvate.
It combines with carbon to form carbon dioxide.
BI.w: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor of the electron transport chain; it picks up electrons and hydrogen ions to form water.

n.1: Pyruvate is oxidized to acetyl-CoA by NAD+ in the matrix, releasing CO2; oxygen is not used in this step.
n.2: Glycolysis splits glucose into pyruvate without using any oxygen.
n.3: The CO₂ exhaled comes from carbon in glucose released during pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle, not from the oxygen breathed in.

BI.q: A geneticist studies pairs of genes in fruit flies. Which pair of genes would be least likely to follow Mendel's law of independent assortment?
o: Two genes, one on the X chromosome and one on an autosome
Two genes lying next to each other on one chromosome
Two genes at opposite ends of one long chromosome
Two genes on different chromosomes that both affect eye color
BI.w: Independent assortment holds for genes on different chromosomes, and nearly so for genes far apart on one chromosome, because crossing over separates them. Genes right next to each other are linked and are usually inherited together.

n.0: The X chromosome and an autosome are different chromosomes, so these genes assort independently.
n.2: Genes far apart on one chromosome are separated by crossing over so often that they assort almost independently. Adjacent genes rarely are.
n.3: Genes on different chromosomes assort independently even when they influence the same trait.

BI.q: A red-haired bull and a white-haired cow produce roan calves, whose coats mix separate red hairs and white hairs. Which pattern of inheritance explains the roan coat?
BI.w: In codominance both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote; roan cattle show both red hairs and white hairs side by side.

n.0: Coat color here is inherited the same way in both sexes; the cross does not involve a sex-chromosome pattern.
n.1: Incomplete dominance would give a single blended color (for example, pink hairs), not separate red and white hairs.
n.3: Multiple alleles means more than two alleles in the population; only two (red and white) are involved here.

BI.q: A lab analysis of a nucleic acid sample detects the bases adenine, guanine, cytosine and uracil. Which other feature would this molecule be expected to have?
o: Deoxyribose as the sugar in each nucleotide
A double helix held by A-T base pairs
Ribose as the sugar in each nucleotide
BI.w: Uracil marks the molecule as RNA. RNA nucleotides contain the sugar ribose, and RNA is usually single-stranded.

n.0: RNA has uracil in place of thymine; uracil pairs with adenine.
n.1: Deoxyribose is the sugar of DNA. A molecule containing uracil is RNA.
n.2: A double helix with A-T pairs describes DNA, which contains thymine, not uracil.

BI.q: Two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt x Tt) are crossed, where tall is dominant over short. What is the expected phenotype ratio among the offspring?
BI.w: Tt x Tt gives 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt. TT and Tt both look tall, so the phenotype ratio is 3 tall : 1 short.

n.1: 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt is the genotype ratio, not the phenotype ratio.
n.2: 1 : 1 is the result of a test cross (Tt x tt), not of Tt x Tt.
n.3: A 1 : 2 : 1 phenotype ratio with an intermediate form comes from incomplete dominance. Here tall is completely dominant, so Tt plants are tall.

BI.q: Sweating cools a runner during a long race. Which property of water most directly explains the cooling?
BI.w: Evaporating water absorbs a large amount of heat (high heat of vaporization), carrying heat away from the skin: evaporative cooling.

n.1: Specific heat is resistance to temperature change; the cooling here comes from evaporation.
n.2: Adhesion keeps sweat on the skin but does not remove heat.
n.3: Water's freezing point does not affect cooling of the skin on a warm day.

BI.q: A microbe from a hot spring lacks a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, yet genetic testing shows it is not a bacterium. How should it be classified?
o: As a virus, since it lacks organelles
As a eukaryote in the protist group
As a fungus, since it has a cell wall
As a prokaryote in domain Archaea
BI.w: Prokaryotes include two groups, Bacteria and Archaea. A cell with no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles that is not a bacterium is an archaeon.

n.0: Viruses are not cells at all. This microbe is a cell with ribosomes and a membrane, so it is not a virus.
n.1: Protists are eukaryotes, so they have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
n.2: Fungi are eukaryotes with a nucleus, so a cell without a nucleus cannot be a fungus.

BI.q: The DNA double helix has the same width along its entire length. Which feature of base pairing explains this uniform width?
o: Each base pair joins a purine with a pyrimidine.
Adenine pairs with guanine, both double-ring bases.
Each base pair joins two single-ring pyrimidines.
Each base pair joins two double-ring purines.
BI.w: Every pair joins a double-ring purine (A or G) with a single-ring pyrimidine (T or C), so each rung of the ladder is the same width.

n.1: Adenine pairs with thymine, not guanine; A-G pairing is a common error.
n.2: Two pyrimidines would make a pair narrower; each pair contains one purine.
n.3: Two purines would make a pair wider than the others; A pairs with T and G pairs with C.

BI.q: A pea plant has purple flowers and the genotype Pp, where P (purple) is dominant over p (white). Which statement about this plant is correct?
o: It is heterozygous, and purple is its phenotype.
It is homozygous, and Pp is its phenotype.
It is heterozygous, and purple is its genotype.
It carries two different genes for flower color.
BI.w: Pp has two different alleles, so the plant is heterozygous. Its genotype is Pp; its observable trait (phenotype) is purple flowers.

n.1: Homozygous means two identical alleles (PP or pp), and Pp is a genotype, not a phenotype.
n.2: Genotype and phenotype are swapped: Pp is the genotype and purple is the phenotype.
n.3: Pp is two different alleles of one gene, not two different genes.

BI.q: In a five-step metabolic pathway, the final product binds to the first enzyme and slows it when the product builds up. What is this control called?
BI.w: In feedback inhibition, the end product of a pathway inhibits an early enzyme, so the cell stops making more product than it needs.

n.1: Positive feedback would speed the pathway as product builds up, the reverse of this.
n.2: Saturation is all active sites filled by substrate, not inhibition by a product.
n.3: Denaturation is loss of shape from heat or extreme pH, not regulation by a product.

BI.q: An onion root tip slide shows a cell in which identical sets of condensed chromosomes are being pulled toward opposite ends. Which phase of mitosis is shown?
BI.w: In anaphase, sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles, so two identical sets of chromosomes are seen moving apart.

n.0: In prophase chromosomes condense and the spindle forms; chromatids have not yet separated.
n.2: In telophase the chromosomes have reached the poles, nuclear envelopes re-form and chromosomes decondense.
n.3: In metaphase the chromosomes are lined up at the cell's equator, not moving toward the poles.

BI.q: A human cell entering meiosis II has 23 chromosomes, each made of two sister chromatids. What happens during anaphase II?
BI.w: Meiosis II works like mitosis: in anaphase II the sister chromatids separate to opposite poles, giving haploid cells with single chromatids.

n.0: DNA replicates once, before meiosis I; there is no replication between the two divisions.
n.2: Pairing and crossing over happen in prophase I.
n.3: Homologous chromosomes separated earlier, in anaphase I.

BI.q: Glycolysis breaks down one molecule of glucose. Which net products does it form?
BI.w: Glycolysis splits glucose into 2 pyruvate, with a net gain of 2 ATP (4 made, 2 spent) and 2 NADH.

n.0: 4 ATP is the gross yield; 2 ATP are spent at the start, so the net is 2.
n.1: Acetyl-CoA and CO2 come from pyruvate oxidation in the mitochondria, after glycolysis.
n.2: 6 CO2 and 6 H2O are the products of complete aerobic respiration, not glycolysis.

BI.q: One strand of a DNA molecule has the sequence 5'-ATGCCA-3'. Which sequence is the complementary strand, written in the same left-to-right alignment?
BI.w: In DNA, A pairs with T and G pairs with C, and the strands are antiparallel. So 5'-ATGCCA-3' pairs with 3'-TACGGT-5'.

n.0: This is the original strand written backward, not its complement.
n.1: Uracil is found in RNA, not DNA; this is what an mRNA copy would look like.
n.2: This pairs A with G and T with C, which is not how DNA bases pair.

BI.q: A human skin cell with 46 chromosomes completes mitosis and cytokinesis. Which result is expected?
o: Two identical cells, each with 46 chromosomes
Four haploid cells, each with 23 chromosomes
Four diploid cells, each genetically different
Two haploid cells, each with 23 chromosomes
BI.w: Mitosis produces 2 genetically identical diploid daughter cells: 46 chromosomes in, 46 in each daughter cell.

n.1: Four haploid cells is the result of meiosis, which makes gametes, not of mitosis in a skin cell.
n.2: Mitosis makes two cells, not four, and they are genetically identical to the parent.
n.3: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same; it does not halve it.

BI.q: During protein synthesis, one type of RNA carries a specific amino acid and has a three-base anticodon. Which type of RNA is this?
BI.w: Transfer RNA (tRNA) carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon that pairs with the matching mRNA codon at the ribosome.

n.0: mRNA carries the codons copied from DNA. It does not carry amino acids, and the anticodon is on tRNA.
n.2: rRNA is the structural and catalytic part of ribosomes; it does not carry amino acids or anticodons.
n.3: Primer RNA is the short strand primase lays down to start DNA replication; it carries no amino acid.

BI.q: A lab manual describes cell walls built from cellulose, chitin and peptidoglycan. Which pairing of wall material and cell is correct?
o: Cellulose in the wall of a bacterial cell
Cellulose in the wall of a yeast cell
Peptidoglycan in the wall of a plant cell
Chitin in the wall of a mold cell
BI.w: Molds and yeasts are fungi, and fungal cell walls are made of chitin. Plant walls are cellulose and bacterial walls are peptidoglycan.

n.0: Bacterial walls are made of peptidoglycan, not cellulose.
n.1: Yeast is a fungus, so its wall contains chitin rather than the cellulose found in plants.
n.2: Plant cell walls are made of cellulose. Peptidoglycan is the bacterial wall material.
